vulnerabilities.title: Hardcoded API Key
vulnerabilities.description: AWS-style API key is hardcoded in the source code, exposing sensitive credentials.
vulnerabilities.impact: Unauthorized access to AWS services, potential data breach, and financial damage.
vulnerabilities.fix_explanation: Moved API key to environment variable. The secure version loads the key from environment using os.environ.get('API_KEY'). API keys should never be stored in source code and should be managed through environment variables or secure secret management services.
remediation_steps: Remove hardcoded API key from source code
Store API key in environment variables or secret management system (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault)
Rotate the exposed API key immediately
Implement API key validation and logging
Use principle of least privilege for API key permissions

vulnerabilities.title: SQL Injection via String Formatting
vulnerabilities.description: User input is directly concatenated into SQL query using string formatting, allowing arbitrary SQL code execution.
vulnerabilities.vulnerable_code:
sql = "SELECT id, username FROM users WHERE username LIKE '%{}%'".format(name)
cur.execute(sql)
vulnerabilities.impact: Complete database compromise, unauthorized data access, data manipulation, data deletion, and potential server takeover.
vulnerabilities.fix_explanation: Replaced string formatting with parameterized queries. The secure version uses SQL placeholders (?) and passes parameters separately to cur.execute(). This ensures user input is treated as data, not executable SQL code.
vulnerabilities.secure_replacement:
sql = "SELECT id, username FROM users WHERE username LIKE ?"
cur.execute(sql, ('%' + name + '%',))
remediation_steps: Replace all string concatenation/formatting in SQL with parameterized queries
Use ORM frameworks (e.g., SQLAlchemy) that provide built-in SQL injection protection
Implement input validation and sanitization
Apply principle of least privilege for database accounts
Enable database query logging and monitoring

vulnerabilities.title: Pickle Remote Code Execution
vulnerabilities.description: Application deserializes untrusted pickle data from user requests, allowing arbitrary code execution.
vulnerabilities.impact: Complete server compromise, remote code execution, data theft, malware installation, and lateral movement within network.
vulnerabilities.fix_explanation: Replaced pickle.loads() with json.loads() for safe deserialization. JSON is a text-based format that cannot contain executable code. Added validation to ensure the deserialized data is a dictionary and that fields meet expected constraints (type checking, length limits).
vulnerabilities.secure_replacement:
data = request.data
profile = json.loads(data)
if not isinstance(profile, dict):
    return jsonify({"status": "error", "message": "Invalid profile format"}), 400
remediation_steps: Replace pickle with safe serialization formats (JSON, YAML with safe loader)
Never deserialize data from untrusted sources
Implement strict input validation and type checking
Use digital signatures to verify data integrity if complex objects are required
Consider using Protocol Buffers or MessagePack for structured data

vulnerabilities.title: OS Command Injection
vulnerabilities.description: User input is concatenated directly into shell command execution, allowing arbitrary command execution.
vulnerabilities.impact: Complete server compromise, arbitrary command execution, data exfiltration, system destruction, and privilege escalation.
vulnerabilities.fix_explanation: Removed os.system() entirely and replaced with a whitelist approach. The secure version only allows predefined safe commands from a dictionary. If command execution is truly needed, use subprocess module with shell=False and input validation.
remediation_steps: Avoid shell command execution with user input entirely
Use whitelist of allowed operations instead of arbitrary commands
If commands are necessary, use subprocess with shell=False and argument lists
Implement strict input validation with regular expressions
Run application with minimal privileges (non-root user)
Use containerization to limit blast radius

vulnerabilities.title: Template Injection via render_template_string
vulnerabilities.description: User input is directly embedded in template string without escaping, allowing server-side template injection and code execution.
vulnerabilities.impact: Remote code execution, file system access, sensitive data disclosure, and complete server compromise.
vulnerabilities.cwe: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code
vulnerabilities.fix_explanation: Replaced direct string interpolation with Jinja2 template variables. The secure version sanitizes input by removing HTML/script tags, limits input length, and uses Jinja2's autoescaping ({{ name }}) which automatically escapes dangerous characters. This prevents template injection while maintaining functionality.
vulnerabilities.secure_replacement:
name = request.args.get('name', 'guest') name = re.sub(r'[<>]', '', name)[:50] template = "

Hello {{ name }}

" return render_template_string(template, name=name)
remediation_steps: Never concatenate user input directly into templates
Use template variables with autoescaping enabled
Sanitize and validate all user input
Prefer static templates loaded from files over render_template_string
Implement Content Security Policy (CSP) headers
Use template sandboxing features

vulnerabilities.title: Plaintext Password Storage
vulnerabilities.description: User passwords are stored in plaintext in source code, violating security best practices.
vulnerabilities.impact: Password compromise, unauthorized access, credential theft, and violation of data protection regulations.
vulnerabilities.fix_explanation: Replaced plaintext passwords with password hashes using Werkzeug's password hashing functions (PBKDF2-SHA256 by default). The secure version uses generate_password_hash() to create secure password hashes and check_password_hash() for verification. In production, passwords should be loaded from a secure database, never hardcoded.
remediation_steps: Use strong password hashing algorithms (bcrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2)
Never store passwords in plaintext
Move user credentials to secure database
Implement password complexity requirements
Add rate limiting and account lockout for login attempts
Use multi-factor authentication (MFA)
Implement secure session management

vulnerabilities.title: Debug Mode Enabled in Production
vulnerabilities.description: Flask application runs with debug=True, exposing sensitive debugging information and enabling code execution via debugger PIN.
vulnerabilities.impact: Information disclosure, stack trace exposure, potential code execution, and easier exploitation of other vulnerabilities.
vulnerabilities.fix_explanation: Made debug mode configurable via environment variable (FLASK_DEBUG) and defaults to False. The secure version only enables debug mode when explicitly set in environment, preventing accidental production exposure. Also added host and port restrictions.
remediation_steps: Disable debug mode in production environments
Use environment variables for configuration
Implement proper logging instead of debug output
Use production WSGI servers (Gunicorn, uWSGI) instead of Flask development server
Configure error pages that don't expose stack traces
Implement centralized error monitoring

security_recommendations: Implement comprehensive input validation across all endpoints
Implement rate limiting to prevent abuse
Regular security audits and penetration testing
Use security linters (Bandit, Safety) in CI/CD pipeline
